```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96)
```

This vignette works through one dataset from start to finish. The aim is
not only to show which functions to call, but to show *why* limits of
agreement that follow the magnitude of the measurement are needed, using a
setting where the consequence of getting them wrong is concrete: the RECIST
assessment of tumor response.

## 1. The data

`recist_readings` is a synthetic dataset that reproduces the design of a
published multi-reader CT study (Yoon, Yoon and Hahn, 2019): 249 target
lesions, each read by six radiologists in two replicate sessions, with the
longest diameter recorded in whole millimeters. The data are simulated, so
that they can be shipped with the package; they were generated so that the
error follows the pattern observed in that study: measurement error grows
with lesion size, more slowly than in proportion.

```{r data}
library(flexloa)
data(recist_readings)
head(recist_readings)
summary(recist_readings$diameter)
```

In routine practice a lesion is read once by one radiologist at baseline
and once, often by a different radiologist, at follow-up. The relevant
question is therefore: *how much can a single reading change when the
reader changes?* `loa_pairs()` forms the corresponding pairs, one reading
by one reader against one reading by another reader of the same lesion in
the same session (`replicates = "matched"`, the default).

```{r pairs}
p_inter <- loa_pairs(recist_readings$diameter, recist_readings$lesion,
                     recist_readings$reader, recist_readings$session,
                     type = "inter")
p_inter
```

## 2. The problem: conventional limits on these data

Start where everyone starts, with the conventional Bland-Altman analysis on
the original scale.

```{r constant}
f_id <- loa_fit(p_inter, transform = "identity")
f_id
```

The limits are about ±8 mm for every lesion. Now look at the plot.

```{r constant-plot, fig.cap = "Conventional (constant) limits on the inter-reader pairs."}
plot(f_id, xlab = "Mean of two readers (mm)", ylab = "Difference between readers (mm)")
```

The differences fan out: among lesions of 10-20 mm the readers rarely
disagree by more than 4 mm, whereas among lesions of 80-100 mm they
disagree by 15 mm and more. The two horizontal lines are too wide on the
left and too narrow on the right. The decision table says the same thing
in numbers. The overall coverage looks fine (`coverage` ≈ 0.95), because a
band that is too wide at one end and too narrow at the other cancels the
two errors in the total. The coverage by thirds of the pairs ranked by their means (tertiles) exposes it:

```{r constant-cov}
f_id$gof[c("hetero_rho", "hetero_p", "coverage", "cov_low", "cov_mid", "cov_high")]
```

Nearly every difference among small lesions is inside the limits and
roughly one in eight among large lesions is outside.

### Why this matters

Limits of agreement are used to decide whether an observed difference is
more than measurement error. Under RECIST 1.1, progression is declared
when the sum of the diameters of the target lesions increases by at least
20% and by at least 5 mm, and partial response when the sum decreases by
at least 30%. We take the simplest case, a single target lesion, so that
the sum is the diameter of that lesion. Consider four lesions re-read by
another radiologist. For an increase the upper limit applies, for a
decrease the lower limit (the constant limits are -6.7 to 8.3 mm because
the pairs carry a small bias of 0.8 mm; the variance-component limits used
later are symmetric):

```{r cases-const}
cases <- data.frame(case = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
                    baseline = c(12, 30, 100, 16), followup = c(20, 37, 114, 10))
cases$change_mm  <- cases$followup - cases$baseline
cases$change_pct <- round(100 * cases$change_mm / cases$baseline)
m_case <- (cases$baseline + cases$followup) / 2
b_const <- loa_band(f_id, mean = m_case)
cases$const_limit <- round(ifelse(cases$change_mm > 0, b_const$upper, -b_const$lower), 1)
cases$verdict_constant <- ifelse(abs(cases$change_mm) > cases$const_limit, "real change", "within error")
cases
```

With constant limits, lesion A (12 mm read as 20 mm, a 67% increase and
therefore progression by RECIST) is dismissed as reader disagreement,
while lesion C (100 mm read as 114 mm, a 14% increase, below the
progression threshold) is called a real change. Lesion D (16 mm read as
10 mm, a 38% decrease and therefore a partial response) is dismissed as
reader disagreement as well. These verdicts are wrong, and they are wrong
in opposite directions at the two ends of the size range.

## 3. The remedy: choose the scale on evidence

`loa_compare()` fits the conventional limits on each candidate scale,
back-transforms them to the original scale, and tabulates the classical
diagnostics for every candidate.

```{r compare}
cmp <- loa_compare(p_inter)
cmp$gof
```

Candidates are ordered by the heteroscedasticity correlation `hetero_rho`,
the Bland-Altman check of whether the scatter of the differences depends
on the mean. On the identity scale it is strongly positive; on the
logarithmic scale it is strongly negative (the log over-corrects); on the
square-root scale it is close to zero, and the coverage by thirds is even.
The overlay plot shows all four bands on the same scatter:

```{r overlay, fig.cap = "Back-transformed 95% limits of the four candidate transformations."}
plot(cmp, xlab = "Mean of two readers (mm)", ylab = "Difference between readers (mm)")
```

The square-root band follows the fan-shaped spread of the differences.
It is the scale on which the conventional Bland-Altman model holds, so
the conventional limits computed there, and mapped back, are the ones to
use.

## 4. Definitive limits from the variance components

The pairs above are exploratory: pairs formed from the same lesion are
correlated. The definitive estimates come from the hierarchical model
fitted on the chosen scale by `loa_components()`, which separates reader,
lesion-by-reader and residual variance and reports intra- and inter-reader
limits. As in the original study, 5% of observations with the largest
standardized residuals are trimmed.

```{r components}
vc <- loa_components(recist_readings$diameter, recist_readings$lesion,
                     recist_readings$reader, transform = "sqrt", trim = 0.05)
vc
```

`loa_band()` evaluates the curved limits at any lesion sizes of interest:

```{r bands}
sizes <- c(10, 20, 30, 60, 100, 150)
data.frame(size_mm = sizes,
           intra_95 = round(loa_band(vc$intra, mean = sizes)$upper, 1),
           inter_95 = round(loa_band(vc$inter, mean = sizes)$upper, 1),
           constant_inter = round(loa_band(f_id, mean = sizes)$upper, 1))
```

A second reader may plausibly differ by about 4-5 mm on a 10-mm lesion
and by about 14-15 mm on a 100-mm lesion. The constant limit of 8 mm
overstates the error at the small end and understates it at the large
end.

### How precise are the limits?

The limits are estimates. For independent pairs `loa_fit()` reports the
approximate confidence intervals of Bland and Altman (standard error of a
limit about 1.71 s/sqrt(n), t distribution), in `f$ci_t`. The inter-reader
pairs above share lesions, so that approximation overstates the precision;
`nboot > 0` replaces it by a cluster bootstrap that resamples lesions.
Compare the two for the constant limits:

```{r ci-pairs}
f_id$ci_t                                   # Bland-Altman approximation
f_idb <- loa_fit(p_inter, transform = "identity", nboot = 200, seed = 1)
f_idb$ci_t                                  # cluster bootstrap (lesions)
```

The bootstrap interval is about three times wider: 7470 correlated pairs
carry the information of about 249 lesions, not of 7470 independent pairs.
For the definitive model, `loa_components(nboot = )` resamples lesions and
refits the model on each resample (a few hundred resamples take minutes;
we use 100 here to keep the vignette quick, 500 in the paper). The
interval end points are back-transformed by `loa_band(ci = TRUE)`, which
gives a pointwise confidence band around each curved limit, and
`plot(ci = TRUE)` shades it:

```{r components-boot, cache = FALSE}
vcb <- loa_components(recist_readings$diameter, recist_readings$lesion,
                      recist_readings$reader, transform = "sqrt",
                      trim = 0.05, nboot = 100, seed = 1)
vcb$varcomp_ci
round(loa_band(vcb$inter, mean = c(10, 30, 100), ci = TRUE), 2)
```

```{r ci-plot, fig.cap = "Square-root limits of the inter-reader pairs with pointwise 95% confidence bands (cluster bootstrap)."}
f_sqb <- loa_fit(p_inter, transform = "sqrt", nboot = 200, seed = 1)
plot(f_sqb, ci = TRUE, xlab = "Mean of two readers (mm)",
     ylab = "Difference between readers (mm)")
```

What the interval adds is a statement of how sure the data allow us to be.
The inter-reader limit at 100 mm is about 14.4 mm with a 95% band of
roughly 13.8 to 14.9 mm: if the clinically acceptable difference at that
size is 15 mm, the whole band lies inside it and interchangeability is
supported by the data rather than by the point estimate alone; if the
acceptable difference is 14 mm, the point estimate exceeds it and the band
confirms that the excess is real. One caveat: the bootstrap resamples
lesions, so it reflects the sampling of lesions but treats the six readers
as fixed; the reader variance is estimated from these six readers only,
and a study with few readers should say so.

## 5. What changes in the decisions

Re-assess the four lesions with the curved inter-reader limits:

```{r cases-curved}
cases$curved_limit <- round(loa_band(vc$inter, mean = m_case)$upper, 1)   # symmetric limits
cases$verdict_curved <- ifelse(abs(cases$change_mm) > cases$curved_limit, "real change", "within error")
cases$RECIST <- ifelse(cases$change_pct >= 20 & cases$change_mm >= 5, "PD",
                       ifelse(cases$change_pct <= -30, "PR", "SD"))
cases[, c("case", "baseline", "followup", "change_mm", "change_pct", "RECIST",
          "const_limit", "verdict_constant", "curved_limit", "verdict_curved")]
```

Lesion A is now recognized as a real change and lesion C as reader
disagreement. Lesion B, near the size where the curved band crosses the
constant limit, is judged the same way by both. Lesion D, the partial
response in a small lesion, is recognized as a real change: at that size
the curved limit is narrower than the constant one. The confidence bands
show that these verdicts do not hinge on sampling error: the change of
lesion A (8 mm) exceeds even the upper confidence limit of the curved
limit at its size, the change of lesion C (14 mm) lies below its lower
confidence limit, and the change of lesion D (6 mm) exceeds the upper
confidence limit at its size.

```{r cases-ci}
round(loa_band(vcb$inter, mean = m_case, ci = TRUE)[, c("mean", "upper", "upper_lo", "upper_hi")], 2)
```

The same comparison over the whole size range shows where a change that
meets a RECIST criterion can be produced by reader disagreement alone.
Because the limits depend on the mean of the two readings, the increase
from a baseline diameter `b` that is still within the limits is obtained by
solving `f(b + D) - f(b) = L` on the square-root scale (equivalently, by
evaluating the band at `b + D/2`), and the decrease by solving
`f(b) - f(b - D) = L`. The progression threshold is `max(20% of b, 5 mm)`,
so it is flat at 5 mm below 25 mm; the response threshold is 30% of `b`.

```{r decision-plot, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "Change at re-reading that is distinguishable from inter-reader error, constant versus curved limits, against the RECIST thresholds for progression (above) and partial response (below)."}
grid <- seq(10, 160, by = 1)          # measurable target lesions: >= 10 mm
L_sqrt <- vc$inter$loa_t[["upper"]]
f_t <- vc$inter$spec$f; finv_t <- vc$inter$spec$finv
curved_inc <- finv_t(f_t(grid) + L_sqrt) - grid     # largest increase within the band
curved_dec <- grid - finv_t(f_t(grid) - L_sqrt)     # largest decrease within the band
const_up <- loa_band(f_id, mean = grid)$upper
const_lo <- -loa_band(f_id, mean = grid)$lower
pd <- pmax(0.20 * grid, 5)                          # RECIST PD: >= 20% and >= 5 mm
pr <- 0.30 * grid                                   # RECIST PR: >= 30% decrease
plot(grid, curved_inc, type = "n", ylim = c(-50, 40),
     xlab = "Baseline lesion diameter (mm)", ylab = "Change at re-reading (mm)")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey75")
lines(grid, curved_inc, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick"); lines(grid, -curved_dec, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
lines(grid, const_up, lwd = 2, lty = 3, col = "grey30"); lines(grid, -const_lo, lwd = 2, lty = 3, col = "grey30")
lines(grid, pd, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "steelblue")
lines(grid, -pr, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "darkorange3")
points(cases$baseline, cases$change_mm, pch = 21, bg = "gold", cex = 1.3)
text(cases$baseline, cases$change_mm, cases$case, pos = ifelse(cases$change_mm > 0, 3, 1), font = 2)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 3, 2, 2),
       col = c("firebrick", "grey30", "steelblue", "darkorange3"),
       legend = c("Inter-reader 95% LOA, square-root band",
                  "Inter-reader 95% LOA, constant",
                  "RECIST progression (+20% and +5 mm)",
                  "RECIST partial response (-30%)"))
c(PD_within_error_up_to_constant = max(grid[pd <= const_up]), PD_within_error_up_to_curved = max(grid[pd <= curved_inc]),
  PR_within_error_up_to_constant = max(grid[pr <= const_lo]), PR_within_error_up_to_curved = max(grid[pr <= curved_dec]))
```

Under constant limits an increase that qualifies as progression is within
reader error for lesions up to about 40 mm; under the curved limits, up to
about 55 mm. The 5 mm condition changes nothing here, because the curved
limit already exceeds 5 mm for every measurable lesion. For the response
criterion the picture is reversed: a 30% decrease is within reader error
up to about 22 mm under the constant limits but only up to about 19 mm
under the curved limits, which are the narrower of the two at small sizes.
Constant limits thus let reader disagreement pass as progression in large
lesions and dismiss real responses in small ones. The two bands also give
different answers to the interchangeability question. If the acceptable
difference between readers is set at 15% of the measurement, the curved
band lies within that tolerance only for lesions of about 100 mm and
above, whereas the constant limit would certify interchangeability from
about 55 mm upwards, over a range where the true error exceeds the
tolerance.

```{r tolerance}
tol <- 0.15 * grid
c(curved_ok_from = min(grid[curved_inc <= tol]), constant_ok_from = min(grid[const_up <= tol]))
```

A word on what these numbers describe. They concern a single target
lesion re-read on the same examination. With several target lesions the
error of the sum has to be propagated from the lesion-level model (by
simulation), and measurements on separate examinations add the
variability of the scans themselves, so the thresholds above are lower
bounds for longitudinal use.

## 6. When should I use magnitude-dependent limits?

Constant limits are the identity member of the family, so the question is
whether the data call for more. Four signals answer it, in increasing
order of formality.

1. **The plot.** The spread of the differences visibly widens (or narrows)
   along the axis of the means. If the Bland-Altman plot fans out, the
   limits should follow it.
2. **The heteroscedasticity correlation** (`hetero_rho` in `f$gof` and in
   the decision table): the Spearman correlation between the absolute
   centered differences and the pair means. Judge it by its size, not by
   its p-value, which mostly reflects the number of pairs. As a rule of
   thumb, a correlation of about 0.2 or more goes with a fan that is
   visible on the plot (the identity scale above has 0.25).
3. **The coverage by thirds** (`cov_low`, `cov_mid`, `cov_high`). An overall
   coverage of 0.95 made up of 0.99 in the lower third and 0.88 in the
   upper third means that the limits are wrong at both ends; the total only
   looks right because the two errors cancel.
4. **The clinical criterion.** When the acceptable difference is a
   percentage (RECIST, or the glucose standard ISO 15197 above 100 mg/dL),
   the comparison has to be made at each magnitude in any case, and
   limits that follow the magnitude are the natural tool.

How much heteroscedasticity matters clinically is a question about the
limits, not about a test statistic. Compare the fitted band at the lower
and upper ends of your data with the acceptable difference. In this
example the inter-reader limit grows from about 4.5 mm at 10 mm to about
14 mm at 100 mm, and a constant limit of 8 mm is wrong by almost a factor
of two at both ends; a band that widened by a tenth over the range would
make no practical difference. The check is inexpensive: `loa_compare()`
fits all candidates in one call, and when the identity scale ranks first,
constant limits are confirmed by the data instead of being assumed.

## 7. Summary

On data of this kind the conventional limits are not wrong on average,
they are wrong at every particular size, and the decisions built on them
inherit the error. The workflow in **flexloa** replaces the visual choice
of a transformation by a decision table, keeps the conventional
Bland-Altman calculation intact on the chosen scale, and returns the
limits on the original scale where the clinical comparison is made.

```{r summary-workflow, eval = FALSE}
p   <- loa_pairs(diameter, lesion, reader, session, type = "inter")
cmp <- loa_compare(p)                 # decision table + overlay plot
vc  <- loa_components(diameter, lesion, reader, transform = cmp$best,
                      nboot = 500)          # cluster-bootstrap intervals
loa_band(vc$inter, mean = c(10, 30, 100), ci = TRUE)
```
